pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — beats and moiré.html
pieces.title: Watered silk: beats and moiré
pieces.caption: A peg and a piece of moiré cloth: press Play and one note seems to breathe while the cloth's bands pass in step. Then, a step at a time: a scope measured from the output shows the swell is really in the waveform; the identity that makes it; ink on ink against light on light, mixed and squinted in linear light (the ink band survives the squint, the added-light band and the sound's are outlines only, until something nonlinear reads them: the eye, the hair cell); two Kuramoto-coupled oscillators you can pull until they lock; the ear's filter at 440 Hz; and last a sweep with the numbers hidden and the scale stretched at random, where you mark when the swell turns rough and when you hear two notes. Measured in Node: the outline's rate equals the difference to 0.034% from 0.5 to 150 Hz; the sum's square holds 3 Hz at exactly a² and a half-wave-rectified copy at −9.6 dB, while the sum itself holds nothing there (the arithmetic's floor); the coupled pair matches two directly integrated oscillators to 1.6e-8. Whether it sounds like one note, where it turns rough, where it splits: only an ear can say, and nobody has listened yet. Speakers or headphones; small speakers can add roughness of their own.
pieces.near: Play 440 Hz and 443 Hz together
pieces.remade: 2026-11-08, after the challenge: light on light is mixed and squinted in linear light in the canvas (rendered band contrast, 16 px means of linear luminance: ink 0.738 → 0.608 at a 12 px squint; light 0.006 → 0.001), replacing an sRGB mix (0.27 on screen) and a CSS blur; step 4 adds the eye's compressive response bringing a faint band back (L^0.4: 0.156), as the hair cell does for the beat; −174 dB named the arithmetic's floor and a squared-sum check added (3 Hz at a² = 0.0400); step 5 says the outline's height, not loudness, and names the K/2 coupling form; the test's 'says nothing' became 'says little' (the shuffle stretches the scale about 30% either way).

first.why: Play-first and physically right everywhere I recomputed, but step 4's twin is shown on a confound: the light-on-light cloth is mixed in sRGB values, so the screen emits a real band (luminance contrast 0.27 in my headless capture, against 0.76 for ink) that a reader's own squint or a step back keeps, while the squint slider, a CSS blur that Chrome runs on encoded values, erases it (0.003). So 'the squint wipes them out' holds for the slider and fails for the eye. pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the ghost tone.html
pieces.title: The ghost tone · catch a tone that isn't in the signal
pieces.caption: **Catch a tone that isn't there.** A ghost hunt in five steps. Two tones, 1000 and 1200 Hz; then a probe tone you drag along an op-art field until it stops throbbing, and you mark where it goes still, the way combination tones have been hunted since Tartini. The lines bend only where a tone is really in the air and pulse only where two real tones beat, so a throb the picture never draws is your ear's. Then the signal as sent, read live by an analyser: two peaks and the probe, nothing at 800 or 200 Hz down to the meter's −90 dB floor, your marks in red. Then the ghost runs backwards as the upper tone moves (2f₁ − f₂), with a hidden-spacing round you can fail: a mark within 5 Hz is caught, which a blind guess does 4.4% of the time. Last, two accounts of the ear's ghost set side by side before you listen: the page's (an amplifier pushed hard, so it fades faster than the tones as you turn down) and Goldstein's (it keeps its distance). You record 'there' or 'gone' at each level, on headphones; a soft clipper puts a pushed-hard ghost in the signal for comparison. Which account your ear follows is open. Measured in Node: the sent signal has nothing at either ghost (double-precision zero); through a roex filter and a compressive envelope the dry tones and probe throb at 5 Hz only at −43.1 dB, against −19.5 dB with a real 800 Hz at −20 dB; the clipper's 800 Hz sits 18.3 dB under the tones at full level and falls 1.7–2.0 dB further per dB turned down; the browser's analyser read −19 and −36 dB, which agrees. Whether you hear the ghost, and where the probe goes still, only an ear can judge. Speakers or headphones; volume firm, never painful. Small speakers that distort make a ghost of their own, so step 5 asks for headphones. At 1000 and 1200 Hz the ghost also completes a 4:5:6 chord, which the piece names; the hidden round moves off it.
pieces.near: Tartini heard them on the violin
pieces.remade: 2026-11-08, after the challenge: step 5 now states both predictions (the page's pushed-hard fade and Goldstein's constant relative level), calls the offer open, asks for headphones, and lets a 'gone' record stand as a result; marks are keyed to the hidden round, so an earlier mark at the same f₂ can't be scored; step 3 names the 4:5:6 chord confound; the check's null now runs through a roex filter and a compressive envelope (dry −43.1 dB vs −19.5 dB with a real ghost).

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the hiding place.html
pieces.title: The hiding place · hide-and-seek with a cricket and a loud tone
pieces.caption: **Paint where your ear hides a sound.** Hide-and-seek in four steps. A loud 1 kHz tone sits still while a quiet cricket chirps and hops past it, always 30 dB under it; you hold a red button whenever you can see it chirping and can't hear it, and your ear paints the hiding place. Beside it, the eye's twin: one grey square on paper and on ink, to drag or join, graded shape, not mechanism, as the page grades it. Then the filter bank (ERB widths, roex shapes) with your red beside the model's box; then the loud one turned up and down, tone or noise band, each run kept as a row and read after a full up-and-back pass (about 38 s) so hand lag cancels, against the lab claim that the hiding place grows with level and leans upward (the piece's symmetric model leans one sixth-octave at most, so a stronger lean is your ear's); last, the MP3's bet as a blind trial over a band of noise one filter wide (not the page's tone, because a tone and a cricket just above it beat at 59.5 Hz, a cue the piece names): sixteen trials, eight close (1059 Hz) and eight far (2828 Hz), a coin per trial for whether the cricket chirps, chance 4 of 8 in each place and 7 or more counted as heard, stated before the first trial, both places scored. Measured in Node: ERB at 1 kHz 132.6 Hz; the model hides 794–1260 Hz at the starting level; a trial with and without the cricket differs by 0.0077 dB; the noise band is one ERB wide and stays under the compressor. What you hear, and where your red falls, only an ear can judge. Speakers or headphones that carry 3 kHz.
pieces.near: A loud tone hides a quiet one close to it in frequency

pieces.title: Under the kick · masking in a mix, from Sidechain ↔ Conversation

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the ghost tone.html
verdicts.why: The hunt is good play and the hidden-spacing round is a real test that can fail: a fixed guess is caught at most 11/251 = 4.4%, and a mark dropped anywhere on the 150–990 Hz strip only 1.25%. Two fixes. (1) Step 5 states Goldstein's rule as settled ('the ear's ghost keeps about the same distance') and never says the page says 'pushed hard'. Then it explains away the one result that would favour the page: 'if it vanishes with the clipper off… suspect your speakers'. So the ear arm can only confirm the offer. Rewrite it to give both predictions first: the page's 'pushed hard' says the ear's ghost fades like the clipper's; Goldstein's abstract says it holds its distance. Say this is an open offer against the page, ask for headphones for the clipper-off runs, and let a 'gone' record stand as a result, with speakers named only as a caveat. (2) Marks are keyed by f₂, not by round. If the hidden f₂ lands on a 10 Hz slider value the reader already marked at (26 of 251 draws), the old marks show bright red and count in 'marks this round'. Reveal can then score an old mark made with the spacing shown. Tag each mark with a round id, or clear it on hide.
verdicts.second: Read as it stands: marks now carry a round id (scored, counted and drawn bright only for m.round === S.round), so a hidden f₂ on a 10 Hz value no longer brings back old marks; step 5 gives both accounts, calls the offer open, asks for headphones, and says a 'gone' counts for the page's account, so the ear arm can come out against the offer; step 3 names the 4:5:6 chord. Note: a few hidden draws still land near simple ratios (f₂ 1250, 1333), so 'moves the pair off such ratios' is mostly true, not always.

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the hiding place.html
verdicts.why: The best opening in the section. The eye watches the cricket chirp the whole time while the ear loses it, and the reader paints the hiding place in red. The twin is kept at 'shape, not mechanism' in its own words. The blind bet scores both places, states chance (4 of 8) and its rule (7 or more) first, and any answer strategy that ignores the sound hits 7+ in 9/256 of runs. Notes, not remakes: the bet uses a tone masker, though step 3 itself says beats can give a cricket away. Close in, the cricket makes 59.5 Hz fluctuation of depth 0.032 (−30 dB), around the AM detection threshold, so offer the noise band for the bet or name the cue. Tell the reader that a lean run should cover a full up-and-back pass (38 s), so reaction lag cancels before red is read as an upward lean.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — binaural beats.html
pieces.title: Two earpieces
pieces.caption: Headphones. A listening head seen from above: put the earpieces on (440 Hz left, 443 Hz right), lift one, and the wobble in the middle of the head should go. Then the Pulfrich pendulum, drawn to scale because a screen can't dim one eye (hold a sunglass lens over one eye and watch the swinging bob); each ear alone; the interaural phase the brainstem compares, live; the beat in the air beside the beat between the ears; and the break: raise the carrier until the beat is gone, then check it blind (8 trials, beat or one tone, Δf held to 5 Hz or less and the carrier roved ±50 cents per trial so pitch can't tell the arms apart; chance 4 of 8, 7+ counts, both arms scored). Measured by its check, from the piece's own graph rendered offline: 440.000 and 443.000 Hz, difference 3.000 Hz; each ear's envelope flat within 1%; in the air the envelope swings 94% at 3.01 Hz, same RMS; the trial's arms differ by at most 21.5 cents in one ear at the lowest carrier, inside the rove; the Pulfrich dot sits where the drawn sight lines cross (63.0 cm). Whether you hear the beat, and where it stops for you, only an ear can say.
pieces.near: you hear a beat at 3 Hz that exists in neither ear
pieces.remade: 2026-11-08, after the challenge: the blind trial's Δf capped at 5 Hz and its carrier roved ±50 cents per trial, so a pitch difference can't pass for a beat; the Pulfrich geometry fixed (the dimmed left eye now sees the bob late, and the red dot sits where the drawn lines cross, behind the path).

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — Huggins pitch.html
pieces.title: One ear, both ears
pieces.caption: Headphones. Hiss in one ear and random dots for one eye; press both ears and a tune should appear, both eyes and a shape floats up (free-fuse or red/cyan; the stereogram is made live). Then what each ear gets, how the brain subtracts (play left minus right and hear the tune in the sound itself; subtract the images and see the shape), and the break: fold to mono, widen the band, and a blind up/down trial with a one-ear leak arm and a mono arm. Method: a second-order all-pass (Cramer and Huggins's), gated between notes. Measured by its check: interaural phase −177° at f0 (model −180°), within 6° of 0 outside the band; band 414–468 Hz at Q 8; each ear's spectrum the same within 0.06 dB; the mono fold notches f0 by 19 dB. Retuning a sounding filter put +24.9 dB at the new note into one ear alone, so the piece gates the twist; the gate leaves a smaller cue the other way, a dip at the note halfway through each 25 ms crossfade (10 dB or more at f0 for about 8 ms; −1.4 dB over 10 ms by the check, −3.0 dB by the challenger), and no 60 ms window now differs by more than +1.6 or −4.4 dB. The one-ear arm is there to catch either. Whether a tune is heard, only an ear can say.
pieces.near: made only out of the difference between two ears

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — precedence effect.html
pieces.title: Point to the clap
pieces.caption: Headphones (the default) or two speakers. A clap from both speakers, one 3 ms late, a coin deciding which; you point where you heard it, and each point is recorded as toward the first, the middle, or the late one; then tap a speaker to silence it. On headphones the two speakers are simulated: each reaches both ears, the far ear 0.26 ms later and 6 dB down, so the late speaker's copy arrives in both ears as from real speakers (no room). Then the two arrivals in milliseconds (0–40 ms, click, clap or a synthetic “ta”), and the break: a sweep that finds your echo threshold, a louder late speaker (to +12 dB), and a blind trial that answers one sound at the left, one at the right, or two sounds (picking a side by guessing gets 7+ of 8 3.5% of the time; the late side 7+ times, or two sounds below your marked threshold, counts against the page). Stereo on purpose: the Echo Walk sketch is mono. Measured by its check: every delay exact to the sample, both routes; on headphones each ear gets both speakers at the right times and levels (3 ms: left ear 0 and 3.25 ms ×0.5, right ear 0.25 ms ×0.5 and 3 ms); the limiter never reached (−1.98 dBFS at the worst, threshold −1). Where the sound sits, and your threshold, only an ear can say.
pieces.near: is heard only from the first
pieces.remade: 2026-11-08, after the challenge: on headphones the two speakers are now simulated (each reaches both ears, far ear 0.26 ms later and 6 dB down), not one copy per ear; the blind trial gained a 'two sounds' answer scored against the page below the reader's own echo threshold; pointing at the late speaker or the middle is recorded as a result, not blamed on the wiring.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — Franssen effect.html
pieces.title: Silence the bell
pieces.caption: Headphones or two speakers. A bell rings; tap the speaker it is ringing from to silence it, and it should go on ringing, because that speaker went quiet 55 ms after it began. Then the two speakers' levels in time; on headphones a virtual live room made here, mirrored, and rescaled at the bell's frequency so that once the bell has settled both ears get it at the same level (the onset still favours the start side, 7.2 dB in its first 3 ms). The break: 12 blind trials, 8 bells that move and 4 that stay, in an arm you choose (room or dry, tone or noise, fast or slow crossfade); 7+ of 8 at the start speaker means it held, 7+ at the end speaker means it failed. What Hartmann and Rakerd (1989) and Yost and colleagues (1997) found the trick needs is shown only after you answer (abstracts only). Measured by its check: the first speaker 42.6 dB down at 5τ and silent after; the settled bell's level gap between the ears within 0.15 dB at 300, 750, 1500 and 3000 Hz from either side (this room unequalised: +11.6 to −26.1 dB); the room exactly mirrored. Whether you hear it held, only an ear can say; the dry arm may well break it.
pieces.near: Location is decided at the onset and then held.
pieces.remade: 2026-11-08, after the challenge: the room mirrored and, for a tone, its far-ear room part rescaled at the tone so the settled bell has no level gap (it had run −11.6 to +26.1 dB by tone and side, and at 300 Hz favoured the start ear); the literature moved to after the trial; the default tone moved to 1500 Hz; the caption's ear corrected (the number it described is gone).

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — binaural beats.html
verdicts.why: Two fixes. (1) The blind trial is matched in level (0.000 dB) and duration (3 s each, the same 80 ms ramps), but Δf can go to 40 Hz. There the two arms differ by 77 cents in one ear alone at 440 Hz, and by 46 cents between the ears at 1500 Hz, so a 7+ above 1500 Hz is not evidence of a beat, yet the verdict tells the reader it is and calls it 'worth an offer'. The rule's 'with one earpiece off you should score at chance' holds only for small Δf. Fix: hold the trial's Δf at 5 Hz or less, where the one-ear step is at most 3.9 cents at 672 Hz and less higher up, or rove the carrier per trial; then reword the one-earpiece line. (2) The Pulfrich drawing gets the direction wrong: seen() delays the right eye while the drawing dims the left one and its sight lines delay the left. With 10 ms delay and the bob at centre moving right, the red dot sits at 57.2 cm (in front) while the drawn lines cross at 63.1 cm (behind). Swap xl and xr in seen(). The opening (a head whose earpieces come off, with red only while both are on) is good play, and the test was right to show the page's 1500 Hz line only after the reader marks.
verdicts.second: Remade as asked: the trial's Δf now runs 0.5–5 Hz and the carrier roves ±50 cents per play, so pitch can no longer tell the arms apart, and seen() now delays the dimmed left eye; my own ray intersection and the piece both put the dot at 63.05 cm, behind the 60 cm path, where the drawn sight lines cross.

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — Huggins pitch.html
verdicts.why: The section's strongest piece: hiss in one ear, then both ears and a tune, beside a live random-dot stereogram (disparity sign and anaglyph channels check out); a subtraction you can hear; and a blind trial with a one-ear arm and a mono arm, chance stated, both directions scored. Note for the next round: the gate swaps the +24.9 dB ring for a dip. Crossfading plain noise against its all-passed copy cancels at f0 halfway through the fade: 10 dB or more down for 7.9 ms at f0, and −3.0 dB in 470–520 Hz over 10 ms (mean of 40 noises). The maker's own check logged −4.4 dB in the fade-in window but scores only the upward side. Make the check two-sided and say so in the caption, or do the swap under a short gap in both ears so one ear carries nothing. The one-ear arm plays the twisted noise to both ears, which makes it stricter, so it will catch this if anything can.
verdicts.second: Note applied: the caption names the gate's dip at f0 and the check now scores both directions.

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — precedence effect.html
verdicts.why: Three fixes. (1) On headphones each 'speaker' is one ear, so 3 ms is a one-copy-per-ear interaural delay about 4× the head's ~0.7 ms range. That is not the page's 'same sound from two speakers', where each ear hears both. Render each speaker to both ears on headphones (near ear direct, far ear ~0.26 ms later and a few dB down, as the Franssen sibling already does), or recommend speakers and say what headphones test instead. (2) The blind trial asks only left or right, so 'heard only from the first' cannot come out against it: a listener who hears two sounds will still report the first. Add a 'two sounds' answer, scored against the page below the reader's own echo threshold. (3) 'Point to where it came from' confirms rather than tests: it is unscored, the reveal follows every clap, and pointing at the late speaker gets 'try again, and check left and right above'. Record that as a result instead of blaming the wiring. Delays are exact (3 ms = 144 samples), and +12 dB peaks at −1.15 dBFS, under the −1 dBFS limiter by 0.15 dB.
verdicts.second: It now tests the page's situation: on headphones each speaker reaches both ears (far ear 0.26 ms later, 6 dB down, as the Franssen room does), so lead and lag each arrive in both ears, and the 'two sounds' answer lets 'heard only from the first' come out against it; one note: 'two sounds twice or more' has no chance level or catch trial, so a careless clicker reaches 'against the page' easily, and a mark of it should be read as a prompt to rerun, not a refutation.

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — Franssen effect.html
verdicts.why: The virtual room can give the answer away by level. The two speakers' room impulse responses are separate random draws, not mirror images. Measured from the piece's own render with a one-bin DFT over 1.2–2.2 s, the settled tone's level difference between the ears runs from −11.6 to +26.1 dB depending on the tone and the start side. At 300 Hz both moving directions settle louder at the start side's ear (by 2.5 and 11.6 dB), so a 'held' there is a level cue, not the onset. At 1500 Hz, near Yost's strongest frequency, one direction gets 18.3 dB toward the truth. The stay trials catch only the case where every cue is wrong (0 of 4). Fix: mirror the impulse responses (same seed, channels swapped), show the settled level difference for the chosen tone beside the slider, and correct the caption's '1.4 dB louder at the far ear' (it is the near ear, for start-left only; start-right gives −1.6 dB). Also, step 2 tells the reader that the dry and noise arms fail before step 3 asks where they hear the bell, which can bias the answers. Move the literature after the trial, or let the trial run first. The opening (tap the speaker to silence a bell that keeps ringing) is the best encounter in the section.
verdicts.second: Recomputed from the piece's own render with my one-bin DFT: the settled level gap is now 0.0 dB at every tone from 200 to 4000 Hz from either side (was −11.6 to +26.1); what remains is the room's steady phase between the ears, mirrored but tone-dependent (at 300, 750 and 1000 Hz it leans toward the start speaker for a moving bell, ±83–113°), which is room physics, not a defect, and the stay trials catch it; the 1500 Hz default sits near ±167°, close to ambiguous.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the missing fundamental.html
pieces.title: the missing fundamental, and three ways to break it
pieces.caption: **Three discs wake, each with a harmonic (200, 300, 400 Hz), and a hum arrives with a triangle nobody drew.** Find the hum’s note among four forks before any number is shown; then what is actually playing (a live spectrum, nothing at 100 Hz), the one 10 ms period the three share, and where the eye’s twin parts from the ear’s: turn the 200 away and the triangle breaks while the period stays, which is why the page grades the pair a shape. Then the tests: add the real 100 Hz and take it away, with the bottom buried in noise; shift or stretch the harmonics until they stop sharing a period, and match the pitch you hear against a reference; a synthesized low voice (not a recording) down a phone line. Measured in what the page plays: at 100 Hz, nothing above the measurement’s floor (174 dB under each partial), while a real 100 Hz added at −20 dB reads −20.0; the line takes 57 dB at 100 Hz and 23 dB at 200 Hz. Whether you hear 100 Hz, only your ear can say. Headphones or good speakers.
pieces.near: Play 200, 300 and 400 Hz together and you hear 100 Hz

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the barber pole and the stair.html
pieces.title: the barber pole and the stair, with a Risset glide
pieces.caption: **Spin a barber pole by hand; a walker climbs a Penrose stair; a tone rises with both and gets nowhere.** The tone is a small Risset glide of my own, eight sines an octave apart in a raised-cosine window, made only to sit under the twin: the full build, stage by stage with its seam tested blind, is the Shepard Tone Synthesizer’s, gathered beside this. The reveal shows what really turns (the voices; a pole turning sideways; a stair that is a real spiral seen from the one view where its ends meet), and the break takes the window off for the ear and walks round the stair for the eye. Checked: the stripes rise as the tone rises (an edge moves up 3 px for +0.05 octave) while the surface turns sideways; voices exactly octaves apart, a wrapping voice at least 84 dB down at any frame rate (96 dB at 60 frames a second), the mix’s level constant to 1e-15, the stair’s ends 0 apart from the special view and 0.74 of a step apart 15° round. Whether it climbs for you, only your ear can say.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the tritone vote.html
pieces.title: the tritone vote
pieces.caption: **Two notes, two arrows: up or down?** Beside them a dress of my own drawing in a glare, standing in for the 2015 photograph, which can’t be used here and which this drawing may not match: it has its own vote. Then what a Shepard tone is, why C to F♯ is exactly half the circle, and Deutsch’s finding as the page gives it. Last, thirty-two pairs with the rules stated first: eight two-semitone catch pairs scored for the short way (7 of 8, 3.5 % by chance), and six opposite tritone pairs each heard four times (C then F♯ twice, F♯ then C twice), a pair counting when its answers are consistent and opposite: 4 of 6, 0.30 % by coin, and never by pressing one button. A short run reads “not shown”, not “against the page”. Drawn as your own pitch-class circle. It never says which tritone answer is right. verdicts.why: Everything holds except the consistency rule. The catch arm is sound: 4 up and 4 down, 7 of 8 is 3.5 %, and response bias cannot pass it. The tritone arm can be passed by response bias. pieces.title: The gallop
pieces.caption: Auditory streaming in five steps. A low-high-low gallop drawn as dots you drag: up and down pulls the two pitches apart, sideways squeezes the time, and the dots regroup into two rows in the eye as you go. Then the signal (two sines either side of 1000 Hz, 40 ms tones, slot time 50–300 ms), the twin in the eye with its grade kept at mechanism, arguably, and Remez's objection, Bregman's three rules with a playable timbre, and last your own boundary: speeding-up and slowing-down runs at gaps from 1 to 14 semitones, drawn as your two lines once each run ends (nothing on screen moves during a run, and its start is held a random 0–4 s). The slope rule is set before you mark: Kendall's τ ≥ 0.6 over four or more gaps, which random marks reach 16.7% of the time with four gaps and 6.8% with six. Van Noorden's numbers are not drawn. Measured: timing, pattern, frequencies, ramps, RMS match, the ramp's ends. Where it splits is only for an ear; nobody has listened yet.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — behind the fence.html
pieces.title: Behind the fence
pieces.caption: The continuity illusion beside Bregman's own twin. A cat behind a picket fence, and a 1000 Hz tone behind bursts of noise. You play it and say what the tone did before anything is explained; then lift the fence, and both were only ever slices. Then the sound analysed in the page, the bet the hearing makes, and three tests. Bring the fence down 2 dB a loop and mark where the gaps show; the plot stays blank during the run, then compares your mark with where the noise could just mask the tone (about +3 dB, from a critical ratio taken from standing knowledge). Move the noise band off the tone at the same loudness, read through a roex filter shaped like the ear's. And a blind test of a tone really there against one filled in, under the same frozen noise. Measured: a 150 ms gap; the noise in the tone's filter +9.9 dB at +10 on the slider; through roex +0.1 dB at a 1270 Hz centre and −13.4 dB at 1414 Hz. pieces.title: Who rewrites whom
pieces.caption: The page's mirror pair, played both ways. A firefly blinks once and chirps twice: count its blinks (the sound-induced flash, flashing warned first, never more than two flashes in a second). Then a mouth drawn in ink shapes “ga” while a formant synthesizer says “ba”: what did it say? Each half ends in a blind test scored on every arm, its rule set first. The flash test's pad offers 1 or 2; it passes only if two chirps add at least ⅔ of a blink and the reader's eye can tell one blink from two (otherwise it is void, so counting chirps can't pass); a coin passes 3 in 512 (0.6%). The lip test's chance is 13%. Measured: the chirps (7 ms of 3.5 kHz, onsets 57.0 ms apart), the flash schedule, the syllables' F2 onsets (about 1010, 1490, 1600 Hz 20 ms after the release for ba, da, ga) and the mouth's opening at the release. Only an eye and an ear can judge whether the second blink or the da appears. A drawn mouth and a synthetic voice are far weaker than the filmed face McGurk used; the face-shut arm says whether this ba is even a ba to you.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the risset rhythm.html
pieces.title: The Risset rhythm · keep up with it
pieces.caption: **Tap along, and keep up.** Press play and tap with the beat: your tempo readout climbs and climbs while an ink picture that contains itself zooms beside it, and neither gets anywhere. Then the walk: the five layers under a loudness window, drawn as the Shepard window moved onto tempo; the same five rates moved up seven octaves into a Shepard–Risset glissando, to put tempo and pitch on one axis; the window opened flat and the crossfade stopped, so the seam can be heard and seen; and a blind trial, press when the loop restarts, page's window against stopped crossfade, ten trials an arm, no clock on screen, chance stated first: 26 % for a reader who presses mid-loop without listening, and a heard seam set as 6 or more hits of 10. Measured in Node on the page's own engine: every layer exactly double the one below, an 11.09 s loop, a window whose summed power is the same at every moment (1.875), level continuous across the seam, and each layer's beats running on into the next layer's as one accelerating stream. Whether the seam is heard is the ear's to say. Speakers are fine. The zoom is the twin by shape only: same loop, other machinery.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — click into pitch.html
pieces.title: Click into pitch · spin it till it sings
pieces.caption: **A flywheel with a card in its teeth.** Spin it up until the taps become a note and mark it; let it coast down until they are taps again and mark that. A lamp beside it can pulse with each click, its brightness a smooth wave: it carries a flashing warning, stays unlit until you light it, and is held at 3 flashes a second unless you choose more. Then the numbers come out against the page's zones, the clicks are shown as one signal at every rate (a comb in time, a comb in frequency), the eye gets its turn, and a blind trial asks taps or tone for twenty unseen bursts, a coin's 50 % shown in every band; a verdict is read only when one split explains 16 or more of 18 answers, and the page states first that random answers would come out 'agrees' 19 % of the time and 'against' 81 %. Measured: the dial is 2·100^p (2, 20, 200 clicks a second), level is held constant in power, the lamp's cap and screen limit switch where stated, and the sine lamp adds no slow false shimmer on a 60 Hz screen, where a one-frame on-off flash added one at about −9.5 dB from 17 to 22 a second. The screen limits the eye's half: the piece measures the refresh rate with requestAnimationFrame (59.9 frames a second in headless Chromium) and its flicker turns to the screen's own steady average at 29.4 a second on a 60 Hz screen, below where a bright light usually fuses, so the eye's fusion shows only at low contrast. Where taps turn to tone, and when the lamp looks steady, only the reader can say.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the waterfall.html
pieces.title: The waterfall
pieces.caption: Stand by a drawn waterfall for 20 seconds while a sound climbs beside it, then both stop, and you say what the stopped water and the sound did. Then the sound taken apart (120 sines under a ripple that drifts up the octaves), a cartoon of the tired detectors with chosen numbers, and a test in two blocks, the still ripple first as the control, then the climb: each opens with an adaptation you choose up to three minutes (the page asks for a few; the piece asks the kit to keep playing for a trial), each trial tops up 8 s, then the ripple drifts by a hidden amount (−0.15 to +0.15 oct/s) and you say up or down. The score is how far the climb moves your point of no motion; answers that ignore the sound reach the 0.15 oct/s rule 5.9% of the time, and the piece says what no audible-adaptor test can rule out. Measured in Node from the worklet's output: the climb at 0.500 oct/s, still at 0.0002, every hidden test drift within 0.004 oct/s, the stop at 20.00 s. Whether anything seems to move only an ear and an eye can say. Opened as a file, it says its sound engine can't load and the walk still works.

pieces.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the ghost in the gap.html
pieces.title: The ghost in the gap
pieces.caption: One red shape that is also the noise's spectrum: stare into its gap for 20 seconds while pink noise with a band cut out plays, then white paper and silence, and say whether a ghost came in the eye, a tone in the ear, or nothing. Then the hole itself (sliders for centre and width), two cartoons that keep the page's hedge (shape for certain; mechanism likely different, since vision's is fatigue and this may not be, and is still argued), the section's tinnitus and musical ear syndrome drawn and not played, with Charles Bonnet as a dashed figure labelled not there, and a test: eight trials, four with a gap hidden anywhere within 1.25 octaves of your setting and four plain. Before trial one it prints both chances: the tone-or-nothing rule 14.5% for random answers (and what it can't rule out), and the pitch match against the hidden gap (47% for a reader matching at their own slider, 22% at random, at the default gap; matches count as a fingerprint only under 5%). Measured in Node at 44.1 and 48 kHz: the gap's bins at the 32-bit floor over the whole loop, and deeper than −100 dB in the gap's middle in every 8192-sample slice (worst −103.5 dB); edges within one bin; both arms −20.000 dBFS; a seamless loop. Whether a tone is heard, and where, only an ear can say; nothing is an honest answer.

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the waterfall.html
verdicts.why: The encounter is right: a place, eyes on a cross, both senses adapted in one breath, red meaning 'moving now'. Three things need fixing in one round. (1) The test is open to a leak. The arm is audible (you hear the climb) and the page states the answer ('it seems to drift down'), so a reader who answers from the prediction says 'down' after the climb and 'still' after the still ripple, scores A − C = 4, and is told 'the aftereffect showed for you'. The rule's own line, that the still arm catches 'a prediction answering instead of an ear', is false: the still arm only catches a habit of saying 'down' in both arms. Fix: give the test part a small hidden real drift on most trials (for example −0.15, −0.05, 0, +0.05, +0.15 oct/s) and score how far the reader's point of 'no motion' shifts after the climb against after the still ripple, in oct/s. A reader who answers from the prediction gives themselves away on the trials that truly climb. Then state its chance before trial one, and say plainly what no audible-adaptor design can rule out. (2) The 45 s ceiling is self-imposed. The kit gives a piece RichPiece.capAfter(s) and RichPiece.hold(), so the piece can offer the page's 'few minutes' (Shu et al. adapted for minutes), either as one long first adaptation followed by short top-ups, run in blocks with the still block first, or as a 2–3 minute option. As it stands, every null comes from 20 s, a small fraction of the page's adaptation, and the opening's 'stood still' reply blames the ear's weakness rather than the short adaptation. That reply also adds a claim the page doesn't make ('reported weaker than the eye's'); either source it in the Context or say 'twenty seconds is far short of the page's few minutes'. (3) The piece breaks if the worklet fails to load. Opened on its own from file://, Chromium refuses the Blob worklet ('Unable to load a worklet's module'). After that, ctx exists and node is null, so every Back or Next throws in stopAll (node.port) and the walk is stuck on step 1, and any later Play would throw the same way. Guard node in stopAll and play, and make ctx only after addModule succeeds. On a secure sandboxed frame, the way the face serves it, it loads clean. Smaller, at the maker's taste: with the eyes held on the cross, the rocks fall on unadapted retina. Ask about the stopped water too, or tell the reader to look at the rock beside the cross when the water stops.
verdicts.second: Keep: the test now scores a shift in the point of no motion against hidden real drifts, with a still-ripple control block first, and my own enumeration gives the same 5.9% chance the piece prints (p = 0.5 is also the worst lean). The leak from answering by the page is named, not closed: answering 'down' to everything after the climb puts the point at +0.20 and passes, and the piece says before trial one that it cannot rule this out. Adaptation now reaches 3 min under RichPiece.hold, and from file:// it now runs clean, with the engine error shown and every step working.

verdicts.file: Auditory Illusions — rich — the ghost in the gap.html
verdicts.why: The lamp that is its own spectrum, with an afterimage and a possible Zwicker tone in the same dark, is the section's best encounter, and the tinnitus, musical ear and Charles Bonnet step is honest: nothing is played, the figure is dashed and labelled 'not there', and the grade is quoted right. Three faults. (1) The pitch match, which the verdict calls 'the tone's fingerprint, not a guess at the slider', is not a fingerprint. The gap moves at most ±0.5 octave, but a match counts as in the gap anywhere within the gap's edges ±1/6 octave, so a reader who always matches at their own slider centre lands 'in the gap' 100% of the time at the default 1-octave width (and at any width from 0.667 octave up), 83% at 0.5 octave and 58.5% at 0.25. A log-uniform random matcher lands in 25%. Widen the hidden jitter well past the scoring window, or score how close each match is to the true centre against the slider centre, and state the guesser's hit rate before trial one. (2) The tone or nothing rule has no stated chance and the same leak as the waterfall. 'There is no coin to beat' is not a chance level: a reader answering at random gets A − C ≥ 2 14.5% of the time (p = 0.5, the worst case), and since the hollow hiss gives the arm away (the piece says so), a reader who answers from the page's prediction scores 4 − 0. Print the 14.5% and say that this count only rules out a habit of saying 'tone', not the prediction; let the fixed match carry the weight. (3) Step three asserts more than the page does. The page says the pair is 'shape for certain; mechanism likely different, since vision's version is fatigue and this one may not be', and that the mechanism 'is still argued'. The piece titles it 'Two ghosts, two machines', calls it 'the same event, built by different machinery', and adds its own proof: 'the eye's ghost sits where the red was, the ear's where the noise wasn't'. That proof sets the eye's position in space against the ear's position in frequency. On the matching axis, wavelength, the eye's green ghost also sits where the light wasn't, which is the Zwicker shape. Drop that argument from the step and the caption, keep the page's own reason and its 'likely' and 'may not be', and retitle it 'maybe two machines'. Also, the caption's '−125 dB or deeper in a 171 ms window' is one mid-loop slice. Across all 62 half-overlapping 8192-sample Hann slices the loudest gap bin reaches −103.5 dB (48 kHz) and −106.1 dB (44.1 kHz). That is still window leakage and inaudible, but say 'deeper than −100 dB in every slice'.
verdicts.second: Keep: step three is now 'One shape, maybe two machines'. It keeps the page's wording (shape for certain, mechanism likely different, vision's version fatigue and this one may not be, still argued) and drops the space-against-frequency argument. Before trial one the piece prints the 14.5% tone-or-nothing chance and names the hollow-hiss leak. The match is scored against a gap hidden within ±1.25 octaves, with guess rates printed, and counts only under 5%. The depth is stated at its worst slice.

offers.what: A sharpening, not a correction: the page's 'gratings laid over each other... really in the image' is already the multiplicative case, and 'mechanism' stands. Numbers: ink-on-ink cloth carries its band as a real component (6 cycles at 0.20 on a mean of 0.27; band contrast 0.94 after blur); the air's sum of 440 + 443 Hz holds no 3 Hz in pressure (the arithmetic's floor), 3 Hz at exactly a² = 0.0400 in its square, and −9.6 dB of its varying power half-wave rectified; light added from two projectors loses its band only in linear light (contrast 0.026 → 0.004 under a 12 px squint), and through a compressive eye (L^0.4) gets one back at 0.16. Candidate Seen sentence, with Loudon's yes: 'The air adds two fast waves and the slow pattern is an outline; overlaid ink multiplies them and the slow band is really in the image. Either way it becomes real where something nonlinear reads it.'

For two oscillators the beat's outline has height 2a·R, where R = |cos(φ/2)| is Kuramoto's order parameter (the identity sin θ1 + sin θ2 = 2·cos(φ/2)·sin(θ̄) in Kuramoto's terms). In the air K = 0, so R sweeps 0 to 1 forever. With the K/N form θᵢ′ = ωᵢ + (K/2)·sin(θⱼ − θᵢ), the swells slow to √(Δf² − (K/2π)²) a second (Adler's slip law; check: 2.598 at K = 0.5Δω, 1.308 at 0.9Δω, 0.597 at 0.98Δω, within 0.2%; challenger recomputed the same and 0.1341 at 0.999) and stop at K = Δω, locked at φ* = asin(Δω/K) (56.44° at 1.2Δω, R = 0.881). With θᵢ′ = ωᵢ + K·sin(θⱼ − θᵢ) the lock comes at Δω/2, so [[Kuramoto Coupling]] should name its form. Candidate sentence: 'The swell's outline is R, Kuramoto's order parameter; in the air nothing couples the two, so it never settles.' Confirmed by the challenger.

offers.section: In the cochlea — the ear is not a microphone
offers.what: "like any amplifier pushed hard, distort it" makes the ear's ghost a product of being pushed hard, and that is the one thing that tells it apart from a speaker's. Goldstein (1967, JASA 41, 676; read at abstract level on the web 2026-11-08, not the paper) found the relative level of 2f₁ − f₂ nearly unaffected by stimulus level, set by the two tones' level ratio and falling sharply as f₂/f₁ grows (about 15–20% of the primaries at f₂/f₁ = 1.10). A device pushed hard behaves the other way: the ghost tone piece's soft clipper puts 800 Hz at −18.3 dB re the tones at full level, −34.9 dB ten dB down, −54.6 dB twenty down (1.7–2.0 dB further per dB; the browser's analyser read −19 and −36 dB). The f₂ − f₁ tone does need high level. Suggested, changing only the simile: 'its outer hair cells amplify sound, and the amplifier bends it at ordinary levels, not only when pushed: the 800 Hz ghost keeps about the same distance below the two tones as they get quieter (Goldstein, 1967); the low one at 200 Hz needs loud tones.' 'What it proves: active and nonlinear' stands. The challenger confirmed the reading (abstract level, clipper numbers reproduced: −18.5 / −34.9 / −54.6 / −74.6 dB). The ghost tone's step 5 lets a listener's records come out for either account. Worth a source check of the paper before it lands.

offers.section: Between the two ears — timing to tens of microseconds
offers.what: The page states the Franssen effect without its condition: “Listeners go on hearing it at the first.” Hartmann and Rakerd (JASA 86(4), 1366–1373, 1989, abstract) found it fails completely in an anechoic environment, tied to how implausible steady-state cues are in a room; Yost, Mapes-Riordan and Guzman (JASA 101(5), 1997, abstract) found it strongest in a live room with mid-frequency tones, strongest near 1500 Hz. Suggest: “In a reverberant room, with a steady mid-frequency tone, listeners go on hearing it at the first.” This would move Franssen off the Context's not-re-checked list. The piece's dry arm can test it by ear; nobody has listened yet. (Challenger: confirmed from abstracts.)

Open question 1 says Huggins pitch is “a few lines of code.” A single pitch is; a melody needs one gate. Retuning a sounding Web Audio all-pass to the next note makes it ring at that note: +24.9 dB in 470–520 Hz in the first 60 ms after a switch to 493.88 Hz, in the twisted ear alone, a cue one ear could hear. Gating it (crossfade the twist out, retune unheard, fade back in) trades the ring for a dip: halfway through each crossfade the plain and twisted noise cancel at f0, 10 dB or more for about 8 ms of a 25 ms fade, −1.4 dB (this check) to −3.0 dB (the challenger) over 10 ms in the band. Band at Q 8: 413.4–468.3 Hz = f0/Q, −180° at f0. (Challenger: confirmed.)

A gotcha for every rich-face piece that makes its AudioContext on the click and plays at once through a DynamicsCompressor (the brief's required limiter): Chrome's compressor starts cold. Measured offline in headless Chromium (and recomputed by the challenger): its output starts at 0.183 of settled at 5 ms, 0.582 at 50 ms, 0.851 at 100 ms, 0.966 at 150 ms, 1.000 by 200 ms; 0.3 s of silence first settles it fully. It also applies automatic makeup gain, ×1.482 (+3.4 dB) at threshold −6 and ×1.068 at −1, so a 'limiter' set this way raises the level too. Unwarmed, the precedence piece's late copy came out up to 8.8 dB louder than set (a click 40 ms late), and the Franssen onset 14 dB under its steady level, the very cue the illusion rests on. These four pieces wait until the context has run 0.3 s before sounding. It also delays everything by 6.0 ms (its look-ahead), equally in both channels. Home: the Web Audio Worklet page, or the rich-face README's piece gotchas.

'Play 200, 300 and 400 Hz together and you hear 100 Hz, a pitch with no energy at it' holds in the air: in what the missing-fundamental piece plays, measured after its compressor, nothing at 100 Hz rises above the measurement's floor, 174 dB under each partial, while a real 100 Hz added at −20 dB reads −20.0 dB. But the page's own Combination tones paragraph says loud tones make an f₂ − f₁ difference tone inside the cochlea, and here f₂ − f₁ = 100 Hz for both neighbouring pairs, the old objection. The cleanest answer is the shift the piece's step 5 runs: shift all three by +30 Hz and f₂ − f₁ stays exactly 100 Hz, while the least-squares residue moves to 109.31 Hz (de Boer's rule about 110 Hz). Suggest: '…a pitch with no energy at it; and it moves when all three are shifted by the same amount, which a difference tone would not, and survives noise over the low band.' The evidence for the clause is the literature (Schouten and de Boer on the shift, Licklider on masking), not this piece: nobody has listened. Confirmed by the challenger.

The gap transfer sentence doesn't say where the gap sits. The illusion is built with the gap at the crossing: in this piece's numbers the two glides are about 150 cents apart at the gap's edges (777 vs 848 Hz at 1.15 s, 823 vs 755 Hz at 1.25 s; the challenger's bisection gives 150.0 cents on both sides). Suggest "a long glide with a short gap at the point where it crosses a short glide with none". The piece's break step lets a listener check that a gap moved away from the crossing stays put; nobody has listened yet. Confirmed by the challenger.

"When something covers a sound" could say what covering takes: noise in the tone's own range, loud enough to have hidden it. Measured: with the band on the tone, the noise in the tone's filter is +10.07 dB re the tone through a roex(p) filter (challenger) and +9.9 dB in the piece's readout. Moved to 2 kHz at the same total loudness (+14.2 dB re the tone), it is −74.3 dB through roex and −82.8 dB rectangular as played, burst edges included; the maker's earlier −115.5 dB left the edges out. Suggested wording: "a burst of noise loud enough, in the tone's own range, to have hidden it". The challenger disputed it as a claim-change: covering already implies it, so it spells out a word rather than changing a claim. It rests on arithmetic and standing knowledge (Warren, Houtgast), not on a listener.

For the Context, § What was checked and what wasn't: a screen can show only part of the flicker-fusion twin. A browser draws flicker no faster than half its refresh rate (measured 59.9 frames a second in headless Chromium, so 29.95 a second; the piece hands over to a steady average at 29.4 on a 60 Hz screen). Even below that, only a smoothly varying lamp is drawn cleanly. An on-off flash is clean only below a sixth of the refresh rate (10 a second at 60 Hz); from there to 30 its third harmonic folds back as a slow false shimmer, about −9.5 dB at 17 to 22 a second. A bright, full-contrast light usually fuses above 30, so on a 60 Hz screen the eye's fusion shows only at low contrast. The ear's half has no such limit (clicks to 200 a second, exactly 1/r apart).
Open question 2 ("Should the page grow a rich face") is answered by Loudon's order of 2026-11-08; the Context still reads it as open. Mark it answered, dated.
